title: The First Letter to Timothy Timeline
sub: Ephesus · Sound Doctrine, Church Order, and the Love of Money
desc: Instructions to a young pastor left in charge of a church drifting toward myths and speculation — covering qualifications for overseers and deacons, care for widows, honor for elders, and a famous warning that the love of money, not money itself, is a root of many griefs.

eras.label: Era One · 1 Timothy 1
eras.name: Guard Sound Doctrine Against False Teachers
eras.dates: A young pastor left in charge of a church chasing myths and genealogies, steadied by his mentor's own testimony of mercy

events.title: Remain at Ephesus, Oppose False Teachers
events.detail: Paul opens by restating the assignment he'd already given in person: stay in Ephesus and stop certain men from teaching myths and endless genealogies that fuel speculation instead of faith.

verses.text: “Myths and endless genealogies, which give rise to mere speculation rather than furthering the stewardship from God which is by faith.”

events.title: The Goal of the Command Is Love
events.detail: Against teachers eager to be experts in the Law, Paul insists the Law's own purpose was to restrain the lawless, not to become an end in itself — the real goal is love from a pure heart.

verses.text: “The goal of our command is love from a pure heart and a good conscience and an unhypocritical faith.”

events.title: Paul's Testimony — Once a Blasphemer, Shown Mercy
events.detail: Paul interrupts the instructions with his own story: a former blasphemer and violent persecutor made the pattern case of Christ's patience, closing in a doxology to the King of the ages.

verses.text: “It is a trustworthy saying and deserving full acceptance: that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, among whom I am foremost.”
“Now to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.”

events.title: The Charge to Timothy — Hymenaeus and Alexander
events.detail: Paul entrusts Timothy with the same fight, grounded in prophecies once spoken over him, and names two men, Hymenaeus and Alexander, whose shipwrecked faith serves as a warning.

verses.text: “Keeping faith and a good conscience, which some, having rejected, suffered shipwreck in regard to their faith. Among these are Hymenaeus and Alexander.”

eras.label: Era Two · 1 Timothy 2–3
eras.name: Order and Leadership in God's Household
eras.dates: From prayer in public worship to the character required of overseers and deacons, closing in an early hymn about Christ

events.title: Prayer for All People — One Mediator Between God and Man
events.detail: Paul calls for prayer even for kings and those in authority, grounded in a striking theological claim: one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all.

verses.text: “There is one God, and one mediator also between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave Himself as a ransom for all.”

events.title: Instructions for Men and Women in Worship
events.detail: Men are told to pray without anger or dissension; women are instructed toward modesty and quiet learning — among the most debated verses in the letter, appealing back to the creation order of Adam and Eve.

verses.text: “I want women to adorn themselves with proper clothing, with modesty and self-restraint… but rather by means of good works.”

events.title: Qualifications for Overseers
events.detail: A detailed character list for anyone aspiring to oversee a congregation — above reproach, one-wife-faithful, sober, hospitable, able to teach, and tested enough not to be a new convert.

verses.text: “It is a trustworthy saying: if any man aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a good work.”

events.title: Qualifications for Deacons
events.detail: A parallel list for deacons and, distinctly, for women serving in that role — dignified, not double-tongued, tested before they serve, with a promise of standing and boldness for those who serve well.

verses.text: “Women must likewise be dignified, not malicious gossips, but temperate, faithful in all things.”

events.title: The Mystery of Godliness — An Early Christian Hymn
events.detail: Paul explains why he's writing — so Timothy knows how to conduct himself in God's household — then quotes what most scholars take to be a fragment of a pre-existing hymn or creed about Christ.

verses.text: “He who was manifested in the flesh, was vindicated in the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.” — six balanced lines, almost certainly quoted rather than composed on the spot.

eras.label: Era Three · 1 Timothy 4
eras.name: Train Yourself for Godliness
eras.dates: A coming apostasy named plainly, and a young leader told bodily training profits little next to godliness

events.title: A Warning of Coming Apostasy
events.detail: The Spirit has explicitly warned that some will fall away, following deceitful spirits and ascetic doctrines that forbid marriage and certain foods — which Paul rejects since everything God created is good.

verses.text: “Everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer.”

events.title: A Good Servant, Trained in Godliness
events.detail: Paul contrasts godless myths with genuine training — bodily discipline has limited value, but godliness holds promise for both this life and the next, because their hope rests on the living God, Savior of all.

verses.text: “Bodily training is only of little profit, but godliness is profitable for all things, since it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come.”

events.title: Let No One Despise Your Youth
events.detail: Timothy's age was apparently a real liability in Ephesus — Paul tells him to counter it not with an argument but with an example: in speech, conduct, love, faith, and purity.

verses.text: “Let no one look down on your youthfulness, but show yourself as a model to those who believe in word, conduct, love, faith, and purity.”

eras.label: Era Four · 1 Timothy 5
eras.name: Caring for Widows and Elders
eras.dates: Practical church administration — who the church supports, who supports themselves, and how leaders are honored and corrected

events.title: How to Treat Believers of Every Age
events.detail: A brief transition verse reframes church discipline as family relationship — older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, older and younger women as mothers and sisters, in all purity.

verses.text: “Do not sharply rebuke an older man, but rather plead with him as a father, to the younger men as brothers, the older women as mothers, and the younger women as sisters, in all purity.”

events.title: Honoring Widows Who Are Truly in Need
events.detail: The longest single instruction in the letter: families are responsible for their own widows first, while the church maintains a formal list of widows over sixty with a reputation for good works, and steers younger widows toward remarriage instead of idleness.

verses.text: “If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.”

events.title: Elders Worthy of Honor, and of Discipline
events.detail: Elders who lead and teach well deserve double honor and legal protection from casual accusation, but persistent sin is to be publicly reproved — and Timothy is told, almost as an aside, to stop drinking only water for his health.

verses.text: “No longer drink water only, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments.” — one of the Bible's most concretely personal, unguarded verses.

eras.label: Era Five · 1 Timothy 6
eras.name: The Love of Money and the Good Confession
eras.dates: The letter closes where it began — warning against those who treat godliness as a business, and calling Timothy to a confession made before witnesses

events.title: Slaves and Believing Masters
events.detail: A brief instruction to slaves under both unbelieving and believing masters — honor is owed either way, so that neither God's name nor the church's teaching is slandered.

verses.text: “All who are under the yoke as slaves are to regard their own masters as worthy of all honor so that the name of God and our doctrine will not be slandered.”

events.title: False Teachers and the Love of Money
events.detail: Paul diagnoses a strain of false teaching that treats godliness as a path to profit, then delivers the letter's most quoted line about money — not money itself, but the love of it, as the root of many griefs.

verses.text: “Godliness actually is a means of great gain, when accompanied by contentment. For we have brought nothing into the world, so we cannot take anything out of it either.”
“The love of money is a root of all sorts of evils, and some by aspiring to it have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs.”

events.title: Fight the Good Fight — The Good Confession
events.detail: Timothy is called a 'man of God' and charged, in language echoing a courtroom, to keep the commandment until Christ's appearing — following the pattern of the good confession Christ himself made before Pilate.

verses.text: “I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who testified the good confession before Pontius Pilate.”

events.title: Instructions to the Rich
events.detail: Having just warned against greed, Paul doesn't tell the rich to become poor — he tells them not to trust uncertain riches, and to be generous, storing up a foundation for the life that is truly life.

verses.text: “Storing up for themselves the treasure of a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of that which is life indeed.”

events.title: Final Charge — Guard What Was Entrusted
events.detail: The letter's last words echo its opening concern almost exactly — turn away from empty, contradictory chatter falsely called knowledge, and guard what has been placed in trust.

verses.text: “O Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you, turning aside from godless and empty chatter and the opposing arguments of what is falsely called knowledge.”
